items.name: arima: ARIMA(1,0,0) with constant
notes: Stata's e(b) contains TWO rows named '_cons'; the second is /sigma. The pairing is positional and listed in extra['pairing'].
Stata's arima reports OPG standard errors, statsmodels uses the analytic Hessian; the observed SE gap is 1e-5..2e-4 relative, consistent with that.

ll/aic/bic agree to ~1e-10, and evaluating statsmodels' ll AT Stata's estimates reproduces Stata's ll (see extra), so both maximise the same likelihood: the coefficient gap is an optimiser stopping point on a flat surface, not a formula difference.

items.name: arima: ARIMA(0,1,1) with drift / e(N) convention
notes: Stata's e(N) for a DIFFERENCED model is the number of usable observations after differencing (tmax - tmin + 1 - d), while statsmodels reports the length of the series it was handed. With d=1 and a tsset sample of 300 that is 299 vs 300 = exactly d.

This changes any per-observation quantity a user computes from e(N) (and it is why ll/aic/bic still agree: they are evaluated on the same differenced innovations). It is a reporting convention, not an estimation difference -- but a script that computes, say, a variance from e(N) will be slightly off.
scalar N rel diff 3.344e-03

items.name: var: VAR(1) coefficients
notes: The name-by-name translation is verified by the agreement itself (<=1e-13 relative); it is not assumed.

Stata's `var, lags(2)` selects ONLY lag 2 (a numlist, not a span). The VAR(2) case therefore runs `lags(1/2)`, which is what westata's lags=2 means. Using the naive `lags(2)` gives a completely different model (recorded in NOTES.md as a trap for users).

items.name: var: VAR(1) standard errors (as reported)
notes: Stata's var uses the ML residual variance per equation (divide by T); statsmodels' cov_params() uses the unbiased one (divide by T-k_eq), where k_eq = 3 is the number of regressors PER EQUATION, with T=299. SE ratio sqrt((T-k_eq)/T) = 0.9949706303 is exactly what is observed for every coefficient, so this is a DOF convention.

items.name: var: VAR(1) standard errors after per-equation ML normalisation
notes: Multiplying westata's SEs by sqrt((T-k_eq)/T) reproduces Stata's ML-based e(V) to machine precision.

items.name: var: VAR(1) e(Sigma) (as reported)
notes: Same DOF story as the SEs: Stata's e(Sigma) is the ML estimate, statsmodels' sigma_u the unbiased one, so the ratio is exactly (T-k_eq)/T per equation.

items.name: var: VAR(1) e(Sigma) after per-equation ML normalisation
var: Granger causality, VAR(1) (Stata vargranger)
notes: westata HAS granger causality (VARResults.granger_causality), but it returns statsmodels' kind='f' result -- an F statistic -- while Stata's vargranger reports a Wald chi2. A caller using it as-is compares an F to a chi2. The westata statistics above are kind='wald'; the F values are in extra.
The residual (T/(T-k_eq)) gap is the same DOF convention as the SEs.

scalar p_y1_to_y2 rel diff 2.587e-01

items.name: var: Granger causality, VAR(1) after ML normalisation
notes: Scaling statsmodels' Wald statistic by T/(T-k_eq) reproduces Stata's vargranger chi2 to machine precision: same test, same df, only the residual-variance DOF convention differs.

items.name: vecrank: yc1/yc2, lags(2), trend(constant), max
items.command: vecrank yc1 yc2, lags(2) trend(constant) max
notes: vecrank stores NO r() statistics (only r(trendnumber)/r(ttext)), so the statistics were parsed from the printed table at 4 decimals. This is the only entry in this domain whose Stata evidence is printed output.
Tolerance is 1e-4, not 1e-9: the Stata side is a 4-decimal print, which is a ~1e-5 relative floor for statistics of this size.

The rank selection rule is applied identically to both sides (smallest r with statistic <= its 5% critical value), so a different selected rank can only come from a different statistic or a different critical value.
5% critical values differ: Stata [15.41, 3.76] (Johansen 1995 tables) vs statsmodels [15.4943, 3.8415] (Osterwald-Lenum).

items.name: dfuller: y_rw lags(2)
notes: Statistic, MacKinnon p-value, chosen lag and N all agree to machine precision -- the test itself is identical.

items.name: dfuller: y_rw lags(2) / printed 1%-5%-10% critical values
notes: Attribution, not hand-waving: dfuller.ado's GetCrit hard-codes a 6-point table (N = 25/50/100/250/500/inf) per deterministic case and interpolates LINEARLY in N, while statsmodels evaluates MacKinnon's (2010) response surface at nobs. The extra field 'stata_table_reproduced' recomputes Stata's printed values from that hard-coded table and interpolation -- if it matches, the gap is fully explained by the table, NOT by a different test or a different statistic.
This does not change any p-value or conclusion (the MacKinnon p-value agrees to ~1e-12), but a user comparing printed critical values would see a 0.1-0.2% difference.

items.name: kpss: y_ar, notrend (H0: level stationary), maxlag 5
notes: Null-direction mapping verified against the printed H0 line: Stata's default is trend stationarity (<=> regression='ct'), `notrend' is level stationarity (<=> regression='c'). Getting this backwards inverts every conclusion, and the two commands use the OPPOSITE null from dfuller.

items.name: arch: GARCH(1,1)
notes: KNOWN DIVERGENCE (the one the old register flagged), reproduced from scratch and now attributed to TWO independent causes:

(a) STANDARD ERRORS -- Stata's arch reports OPG (e(vcetype)='OPG'); westata's GARCH.fit() never passes cov_type, so arch the package's default 'robust' (Bollerslev-Wooldridge) is used. westata's SEs equal arch's robust SEs exactly (separate attribution entry). The SE gap is up to 2.8e-1 relative, which can move a z statistic across a significance boundary.

(b) LIKELIHOOD / POINT ESTIMATES -- the GARCH recursion needs a presample h_0. Stata uses e(archi) = mean of squared demeaned residuals; the arch package uses an exponentially weighted backcast. Different h_0 means a slightly different OBJECTIVE, so the maximisers differ: omega moves most (it absorbs the presample level). extra['ll_at_stata_params_by_presample_h0'] shows that swapping h_0 to Stata's e(archi) reproduces Stata's ll to ~1e-4, while arch's own h_0 leaves a ~1.3e-2 gap at the same parameters.
Significance impact: for this series alpha and beta are significant under both, but the omega z statistic moves noticeably.
scalar ll rel diff 1.640e-05
scalar aic rel diff 1.633e-05
scalar bic rel diff 1.615e-05

items.name: arch: GARCH(1,1) SE convention attribution (robust vs classic/OPG)
notes: westata's reported SEs are identical to the arch package's DEFAULT (robust) SEs, proving westata inherits cov_type='robust'. Stata uses OPG, which is neither the robust nor the classic (inverse-Hessian) estimator, so even cov_type='classic' does not reproduce Stata -- see extra.
This is a convention/cov_type difference, not an arithmetic error, but it is a behavioural difference a user must know about.
